title: Increasing and decreasing functions
competency: Find critical numbers and the intervals where a function increases or decreases.

keywords.def: A function whose graph rises from left to right: x₁ < x₂ gives f(x₁) ≤ f(x₂).
A number c in the domain where f′(c) = 0 or f′(c) does not exist.

en.text: A function is increasing where its graph rises from left to right (f′ ≥ 0) and decreasing where it falls (f′ ≤ 0). Critical numbers are where f′ = 0 or f′ does not exist, inside the domain. Mark them on a sign chart of f′ to see where f rises and falls.

am.text: ፋንክሽን f′ ≥ 0 በሆነበት ይጨምራል፣ f′ ≤ 0 በሆነበት ይቀንሳል። ወሳኝ ቁጥሮች f′ = 0 ወይም f′ የሌለበት ናቸው።

screens.title: Uphill and downhill
screens.ask: f(x) = x². Where does its graph go downhill as you move right?
screens.after:
The slope of x² is 2x.
For x < 0, 2x is negative: the graph goes downhill.
For x > 0, 2x is positive: uphill.
At x = 0 the slope is 0: the bottom of the valley.

screens.title: Increasing and decreasing
paras: if f(x₁) ≤ f(x₂), f is increasing on I;
if f(x₁) ≥ f(x₂), f is decreasing on I.
With < or >, it is strictly increasing or decreasing.
screens.note: A function that is increasing or decreasing is monotonic.

screens.title: The derivative test
paras: If f′(x) ≥ 0 inside I, f is increasing on I.
If f′(x) ≤ 0 inside I, f is decreasing on I.

screens.title: Uphill, downhill: y = x³ − 3x²
screens.ask: The dots lie on y = x³ − 3x². Its slope is f′(x) = 3x² − 6x. Tap each dot.

screens.title: Key words
defs: A function whose graph rises from left to right: x₁ < x₂ gives f(x₁) ≤ f(x₂).
A number c in the domain where f′(c) = 0 or f′(c) does not exist.

screens.text: Find the critical numbers of f(x) = 4x³ − 5x² − 8x + 20 (tap all):
screens.why:
f′(x) = 12x² − 10x − 8.
Factor: 2(6x² − 5x − 4) = 2(2x + 1)(3x − 4).
f′ = 0 when 2x + 1 = 0 or 3x − 4 = 0.
Critical numbers: x = −1/2 and x = 4/3.
f′ exists everywhere, so there are no others.

screens.title: f(x) = 3x⁴ − 4x³ − 12x² + 5
steps: Increasing on [−1, 0] and [2, ∞). Decreasing on (−∞, −1] and [0, 2].

screens.title: Sign chart: test one point per interval

screens.text: Find the critical numbers of f(x) = 2√x(6 − x) (tap all):
screens.why:
Write f = 12x^(1/2) − 2x^(3/2).
f′ = 6x^(−1/2) − 3x^(1/2) = (6 − 3x)/√x = 3(2 − x)/√x.
f′ = 0 when x = 2.
f′ does not exist at x = 0, and 0 is in the domain.
Critical numbers: 0 and 2. (6 is a zero of f, not of f′.)
screens.clue: Also look where f′ does not exist.

screens.text: Find the critical numbers of f(x) = 2x³ + 9x² − 24x (tap all):
screens.why:
f′(x) = 6x² + 18x − 24.
Take out 6: 6(x² + 3x − 4) = 6(x + 4)(x − 1).
f′ = 0 at x = −4 and x = 1.
Trap: −1 and 4 come from wrong signs in the factors.

screens.text: Use the derivative test: f(x) = 2x² + 6x − 10 is increasing on
screens.why:
f′(x) = 4x + 6.
Increasing where f′(x) ≥ 0: 4x + 6 ≥ 0.
x ≥ −6/4 = −3/2.
So f is increasing on [−3/2, ∞).

screens.text: Use a sign chart: f(x) = −2x³ + 3x² + 12x + 6 is increasing on
screens.why:
f′(x) = −6x² + 6x + 12 = −6(x² − x − 2) = −6(x − 2)(x + 1).
Critical numbers: −1 and 2.
Test x = 0: f′(0) = 12 > 0, so f rises on [−1, 2].
Test x = 3: f′(3) = −24 < 0. Outside [−1, 2] f falls.
Increasing on [−1, 2].

screens.text: Find the critical numbers of f(x) = 2x²/(1 − x²):
screens.why:
Quotient rule: f′ = (4x(1 − x²) + 4x³)/(1 − x²)² = 4x/(1 − x²)².
f′ = 0 when x = 0.
f′ is undefined at x = ±1, but f is also undefined there.
A critical number must be in the domain, so ±1 do not count.
Only 0.
screens.clue: Critical numbers must be in the domain.

screens.text: Find where f(x) = x − 6√(x − 1) is decreasing (domain x ≥ 1):
screens.why:
f′(x) = 1 − 6 · 1/(2√(x − 1)) = 1 − 3/√(x − 1).
f′ = 0 when √(x − 1) = 3, so x − 1 = 9, x = 10.
For 1 < x < 10, √(x − 1) < 3, so f′ < 0: decreasing.
For x > 10, f′ > 0: increasing.
Decreasing on [1, 10].

items.text: Factor to find the zeros of x² − x − 12 (tap both):
items.why:
Find two numbers with product −12 and sum −1: −4 and 3.
x² − x − 12 = (x − 4)(x + 3).
Zeros: x = 4 and x = −3.

Factor: 2x² + 3x − 2 = (2x − 1)(x + 2).
Zeros: x = 1/2 and x = −2.
The parabola opens up, so it is ≥ 0 outside the zeros.
Answer: x ≤ −2 or x ≥ 1/2.
Check x = 0: −2 < 0, so 0 is not included. ✓

Factor: (x + 4)(x − 1).
Zeros: −4 and 1.
The parabola opens up, so it is < 0 between the zeros.
Answer: −4 < x < 1. Check x = 0: −4 < 0. ✓

items.text: Find the critical numbers of f(x) = x³ + 6x² (tap all):
Find the critical numbers of f(x) = 2x²/(1 − x²):
items.why:
f′ = 4x/(1 − x²)², zero at x = 0.
x = ±1 are not in the domain, so they are not critical numbers.
Answer: 0 only.

items.text: Find the critical numbers of f(x) = 8x√(1 − x²) (tap all):
items.why:
Domain: −1 ≤ x ≤ 1.
Product rule: f′ = 8√(1 − x²) − 8x²/√(1 − x²) = 8(1 − 2x²)/√(1 − x²).
f′ = 0 when x² = 1/2: x = ±√2/2.
f′ does not exist at x = ±1 (in the domain).
All four are critical numbers.

items.text: Use a sign chart: f(x) = x³ + 6x² is decreasing on
items.why:
f′(x) = 3x(x + 4). Critical numbers −4 and 0.
Test x = −1: 3(−1)(3) = −9 < 0.
So f′ < 0 between −4 and 0.
Decreasing on [−4, 0].

items.text: Use a sign chart: f(x) = (x + 3)²(x − 1)² is increasing on
items.why:
f′ = 2(x + 3)(x − 1)² + 2(x + 3)²(x − 1) = 4(x + 3)(x + 1)(x − 1).
Critical numbers: −3, −1, 1.
Signs of f′: − on x < −3, + on (−3, −1), − on (−1, 1), + on x > 1.
Increasing on [−3, −1] and [1, ∞).

test.text: Find the critical number of f(x) = x² − 6x:
test.why:
f′(x) = 2x − 6.
2x − 6 = 0 gives x = 3.
Trap: 0 and 6 are the zeros of f, not of f′.

test.text: Use the derivative test: f(x) = x³ − 3x is decreasing on
test.why:
f′(x) = 3x² − 3 = 3(x − 1)(x + 1).
f′ ≤ 0 between the zeros −1 and 1.
Test x = 0: f′(0) = −3 < 0. ✓
Decreasing on [−1, 1].

test.text: True or false: if f′(x) > 0 on an interval, f is increasing there.
test.why:
f′(x) > 0 means every tangent slopes upward.
So the graph rises from left to right on the interval.
This is the derivative test. True.

f′(x) = −2.
−2 < 0 for every x.
So f is decreasing everywhere: a line with negative slope.

notes.text: Increasing/decreasing test (p.99) has two misprints: the clause "f(x₁) ≥ f(x₂)" should be "f is continuous on I", and c, d say "f′(x) > 0 and f′(x) = 0", which should be "f′(x) > 0 (zero only at isolated points)". Lessons use the corrected test.
Example 2 writes "increasing on [−1, 0] ∪ [2, ∞)". It increases on each interval separately, not on the union (f(0) = 5 > f(1) = −8); lessons say "on [−1, 0] and [2, ∞)".
